implementation_notes: In the functional stack the connection is http4s' Client[F]: EmberClientBuilder.default[IO].build returns a Resource[IO, Client[IO]] that owns a pooled, HTTP/1.1+HTTP/2 client, and the gateway is a trait/class parameterised by the effect type F (tagless-final) whose methods return F[...] values, decoding with circe/µPickle and translating failures into one domestic error type. Foreign vocabulary (http4s Request/Response, JSON ASTs) never appears in the caller's signature, and because the client is a Resource its acquisition and shutdown follow the program's lifetime rather than a constructor call. Use this variant when the whole application is effect-typed; the plain class form remains the pragmatic choice on Future or blocking stacks.
pitfalls: Effect values are descriptions: nothing runs until the program is run by the runtime, so a gateway method that forgets to sequence the effect returns an unexecuted value (and unsafeRunSync inside library code is the anti-pattern).
The Client is a Resource: using it after the .use block returns a closed connection pool; acquire it once at the application boundary.
Required type-class instances (Concurrent/Async, JSON decoders) must be in scope where the gateway is built - a missing instance fails in the wiring, not in the gateway.

variants.name: Plain class over a JVM client (java.net.http / sttp / Play WS)
variants.implementation_notes: Outside the cats-effect ecosystem the gateway is an ordinary Scala class with constructor-injected dependencies: the JVM client (java.net.http.HttpClient, sttp, Play WS), the base URI and the JSON codec; methods return domestic case classes inside Try or Future, and the translation is written with pattern matching on the foreign payload. Scala's case classes plus copy make the mapping code short and readable, and named/default arguments keep the wiring declarative. Prefer this shape when callers already live on Futures or on a blocking stack: it needs no effect runtime, and the http4s variant only pays off when the whole program is effect-typed.
pitfalls: Try/Future hide failures inside the value: a caller that ignores the failed case never learns the foreign call failed, so the domestic error type must be part of the method contract.
A java.net.http.HttpClient is shared and pools connections: constructing one per gateway instance discards the pool; a single instance per service is the rule.
Implicit JSON codecs are resolved at the use site: importing a different decoder silently changes the wire mapping at one call site only.
